items.title: Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface
items.summary:
Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino ’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab. 

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

Ēclos is designed to support three-dimensional compositions 

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Its patterning runs right through the slab for refined exposed edges

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With…
items.t: Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

items.title: How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design
items.summary:
The sauna is Finnish. The company reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs , based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

At Klafs headquarters, where the company’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he says, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the company describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden…
items.t: How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel , a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake. 

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

items.title: SHoP Architects designs Novak Djokovic-backed Miami supertall skyscraper
items.summary:
New York studio SHoP Architects has released designs for a ribbed supertall skyscraper in Miami , announced alongside the launch of a luxury brand for which Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic is developing amenity facilities. 

SHoP Architects, who are behind some of New York City's tallest buildings, designed the 1,049-foot-tall (320-metre-tall) skyscraper around ATMA, a luxury brand being launched by hospitality operator Aman Group . 

If completed at the stated height, it would be taller than the city's current tallest skyscraper, and have the same projected height as the in-progress Waldorf Astoria Hotel & Residences Miami , which has been cited as the city's future tallest.

The skyscraper will include a hotel, residences and a members' club. According to Aman Group, ATMA's "advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities" will be developed "exclusively" with Djokovic, who is credited as a global partner of the new brand.

Designs for the skyscraper itself show a ribbed form of balconied terraces organised around a central void that runs from the crown to the podium. 

It is planned for Miami's Brickell neighbourhood, and Aman Group said that the floor-to-ceiling windows of the skyscraper will merge the "futuristic architecture with the bay". 

Toronto-based interiors outfit Studio Paolo Ferrari has been chosen as the interiors lead on the project. It will include condos with one to five bedrooms, with six-bedroom penthouses pushed to the top of the skyscraper. 

The structure will have setbacks at the upper floors, presumably to create more panoramic…

items.title: Tiffany & Co. Brings a Century of American Beauty to Crystal Bridges
items.summary:
In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

The Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the company’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

An 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the company’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s…
items.t: Tiffany & Co. Brings a Century of American Beauty to Crystal Bridges

items.title: Fictional Project designs home in Kerala to feel "one with the landscape"
items.summary:
Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala , India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home's built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home's pared-back and open interiors.

"The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape," the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

"The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors," the studio explained.…

items.title: Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.summary:
Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen's 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler . In this interview , we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis , who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

"I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture," Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

The duo met during their studies at Sweden's Beckmans College of Design , where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work "without hierarchies" and maintain creative control of the studio's output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding "universe".

Sabine Marcelis selected Swedish Girls for the 20x20 project. Photo by Nacho Alegre, BD Barcelona 

The Big Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective's tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week .

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

items.title: Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome
items.summary:
A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome , Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a currently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban's signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a "fragmented urban fabric".

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together," said Ban.

"The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a new sense of belonging in the neighbourhood."

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci's proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish…
items.t: Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome

items.title: Waugh Thistleton Architects set to transform derelict bathing pavilion into Tracey Emin-backed studios and sauna
items.summary:
UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms. 

"The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with new spaces for art, culture and the local community," said Waugh Thistleton Architects .

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Westbrook Pavilion in Margate for Tracey Emin 

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

"Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room," said the studio.

"Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character," it continued.

"The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a new sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea."

The pavilion was built in 1914 

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building's core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings…

items.title: Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes
items.summary:
A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed , two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs , WeCanMake , Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their "cutting-edge" environmental prototypes. 

SearoSoft is a seaweed-based earplug 

Described as the "world's first seaweed-based single-use earplug", SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs. 

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic -based products, which can be drying. 

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Local Works Studio has won a grant with Ferment 

Among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings . 

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a "harvest-to-house system", where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery. 

Neighbourhood Factory Futures is a homegrown timber…
items.t: Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes

items.title: Programa software tracks everything from product dimensions to material quantities
items.summary:
Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.

According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on "hundreds of decisions", which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets. 

Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops. 

These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities. 

Programa 's redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs. 

The company explained that increased AI use is making convincing images "easier to generate than ever", yet clients often run into logistical issues when using this alone. 

For example, the AI model doesn't take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space's natural light. 

With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software's organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The company explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it,…
items.t: Programa software tracks everything from product dimensions to material quantities

items.title: Carsten Höller’s Monumental Slides Bring Play to Mexico City
items.summary:
Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara , a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno . The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a new way to move between them.

The slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and…
items.t: Carsten Höller’s Monumental Slides Bring Play to Mexico City

items.title: OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali
items.summary:
What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the new Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA , Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

The architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.…
items.t: OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

items.title: Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.summary:
Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen's 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler . In this interview , the Dutch designer explains why she doesn't find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

"How I think is not typical design," she told Dezeen. "So I'm never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it's just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece."

"I've never been so inspired by design in general," she added. "It's a skill that fits very well to me, but I'd rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline."

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn't have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

"I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them," she explained. "For me, it's sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be."

Tangelder is known for sculptural pieces that play with unusual material combinations. Photo by Alejandro Ramirez Orozco 

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible , as well as winning that year's Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

items.title: Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress
items.summary:
Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art's 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist , a graduate of the Parsons School of Design , employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.

"The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I'm making," Zimbalist told Dezeen.

"Very often I favour the usage of byproducts."

The material's technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.

"My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body," said Zimbalist.

"The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic."

Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term "plastic".

"For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to 'biomaterials'; when people hear 'bioplastic', they tend to focus on the plastic," Zimbalist continued.

"'Biomaterial' opens up a different conversation about what the…

items.title: “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks
items.summary:
Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne ’s public housing towers. In this interview , he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Simon Robinson (centre) is the director of Office 

Announced by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria ’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne's public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN's special rapporteur on housing , and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Flemington Estate has not yet been demolished while a class file action filed by the residents is in progress 

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office .

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility…

items.title: SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration
items.summary:
Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia , USA, "breathing new life" into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

"Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station's strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop. 

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios , 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design .

"First, it came from this game of rejection," he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

"Let's say everyone likes to use wood – I won't have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won't have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that's exactly the material I'm going to use."

"I'll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior," he continued. "I'll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture."

"You can't be safe. You always have to risk."

items.title: ESR x Craig & Karl Bring a Pocket Full of Joy to Everyday Technology
items.summary:
The objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a new collaboration between ESR , a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl —which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal…

items.title: Check In for the Holidays: Inside 16 Imaginative Christmas Suites
items.summary:
Hotel lobbies may feature towering holiday trees and elaborate gingerbread displays, but some of the season’s most imaginative designs are happening behind closed doors. Creative teams are giving guest rooms full seasonal makeovers—blending thoughtful décor with interactive touches. From nostalgic throwbacks to festive retreats, these design-forward suites make the stay itself the destination. Ahead, explore some of the most imaginative holiday suites to check into this season.

16 Festive Hotel Suites to Book for the 2026 Holiday Season 
 The Mills House in Charleston, SC 
 The Watercolor Wonderland Suite creates a whimsical, storybook setting with pastel ornaments, pink-wrapped gifts, and a miniature holiday village. Photography courtesy of The Mills House.

Inspired by the Lowcountry’s pastel façades and historic architecture, the Watercolor Wonderland Suite at The Mills House in Charleston, South Carolina, was created in collaboration with local artist Rebecca Meixner . Original watercolor illustrations of Charleston landmarks, including Rainbow Row and the city’s steepled churches, appear throughout the suite, while pastel ornaments bring a soft seasonal touch to the Christmas tree.

In the Watercolor Wonderland Suite, pink holiday wreaths adorn the bathroom’s geometric tile walls, adding a playful contrast to the black-and-white palette. Photography courtesy of The Mills House.

items.title: Arcadia’s New Almeya Collection Marks A New Era of Flexible Design
items.summary:
Hybrid and remote work have changed what people expect from a modern workspace. No longer do people want fixed seating or single-purpose design. Instead, they are looking for modular, multi-use furniture that boosts productivity while maintaining comfort and style. When Chris and Jon Panichella set out to design their latest seating collection for Arcadia , they turned to everyday life for inspiration.

“The idea for Almeya began with a woman working from an inflatable raft at the beach,” the Panichellas explain. “She could recline and read in one position, then sit up and work in another—a simple moment that captured how much people now expect from their spaces: comfort, flexibility, and function. That observation became the very first concept sketch that eventually evolved into the Almeya offering we know today.”

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

With a full family of products—including modular, lounge, work-lounge, benches, and occasional tables—the Almeya Collection offers a fluid experience that adapts to these modern shifts in productivity and collaboration. Across the series, soft, organic forms invite comfort and ease, while integrated tables, flexible configurations, and strategic power stations allow for both focus and sociability.

Almeya began with a single lounge chair and an integrated two-tiered side table. The idea was simple: the combination could function as a self-contained work island, with two separate surfaces, power access, and an optional rotating tablet. items.title: Not ready for the cold and dark? Maybe you need a ‘winter transition week’ | Emma Beddington
items.summary:
A psychologist has recommended we all take time for slowness and rest, to prepare ourselves for the coming months. It’s a nice idea, but it may prove my downfall

How are you feeling about the rapid dying of the light? Are you already sluggish and glum, poleaxed by the “polar vortex” or seasonal lurgy? That might be because you’re doing winter wrong: according to health psychologist Kari Leibowitz, writing in the Washington Post, we’d all benefit from a “winter transition week”.

Leibowitz, the author of a book, How to Winter, based on her time living in the Arctic, explains: “I intentionally clear out my calendar … say no to extra obligations, try to cancel or postpone unnecessary meetings and make time for rest and slowness.” During this time, she also recommends stocking up on tea, getting out thick socks, eating soup and planning little treats.
